Field key search and writer ranking

Search a stripped executable for a set of serialized keys and rank candidate writers with:

Command
xref -b ./app field --keys c,m,e --write --writes-all-of m,e --json

--writes-all-of retains candidates with observed writes covering every named field on one tracked input root. Wide writes can cover multiple fields. The result remains an instruction-based candidate, not proof of a concrete source type or object lifetime. --min-keys N permits partial key matches; without it the requested key set remains exact. Keys emitted only inside the value of a requested key (for example nanos of an elapsed: Duration field) stay in the layout output but do not count against the exact set. --max-functions and --max-instructions set bounded analysis limits.

The fast seed intersection follows known direct calls. If it excludes partial key-reference seeds, coverage reports key_seed_filter_excluded and an incomplete-analysis warning: indirect or unresolved calls could connect those seeds. Use --exhaustive-key-seeds to include them under the configured function budget. This can take longer and may still be limited by the budget.

Before applying --limit, writer candidates are ranked using the number of field offsets written in the same basic block and the shortest undirected direct-call distance, up to six edges, from the inferred serializer. Stores that start at a field and are no wider than its observed reads count extra (more so when they cover every layout field), as does a field compared before it is written (an update such as cmp r, [p+0x10] then mov [p+0x10], r). Wide stores that span several fields (movups) look like whole-struct copies and get no such credit, and neither does a root whose queried slot is loaded and then dereferenced in the same function, because that slot holds a pointer (for example a Vec {cap, ptr, len}). The JSON fields colocated_written_fields, callgraph_distance and ranking_score show the evidence. Unknown or indirect call relationships have no distance; the rank is a heuristic, not proof that two functions handle the same object.

--writer-root returned|argument|loaded keeps only writers whose offsets are relative to that kind of pointer. Use returned for a struct reached through a pointer returned by a call, such as a map lookup:

Command
xref -b ./app field --keys c,m,e --write --writes-all-of m,e --writer-root returned

Offset constellations like 0, 8, 16 are common (a Vec has the same shape), so on a large binary a writer through a lookup result can rank below many argument-relative candidates near the serializer; restricting the root removes them.

For whole-image searches, XRef builds a reusable index of static references, direct calls and writer facts. It stores private cache files below $XDG_CACHE_HOME/xref/field-index-v1, or ~/.cache/xref/field-index-v1 when XDG_CACHE_HOME is unset. The cache includes instruction text and addresses, is keyed by the input and XRef executable contents, and is rebuilt after a change or corruption. Files are limited to 256 MiB each; old files are not automatically evicted. Delete that directory to clear them. A scoped --within search does not use the persistent index. Coverage fields report cache hits, prefiltered functions and analysis limits. The first search must build the index; later searches can reuse it with different key sets and writer filters.

For many queries over one binary, run the MCP server (xref -b ./app mcp) and send xref_query requests with {"operation": "field", "request": {...}}. The request takes keys, write, writes_all_of, writer_root, limit (default 16), min_keys, min_offsets, max_functions, max_instructions, layout_only and exhaustive_key_seeds, and returns the same JSON report as field --json. The server keeps the image digest, the whole-image scan and call graph, the writer index and analyzed functions in memory, so after the first queries a new key set or filter costs only key matching, context selection and ranking, without the image load and whole-image scan a fresh CLI run repeats. The server starts building this state (including the writer index, when the on-disk cache is empty) in the background as soon as it starts. Queries never wait for that warm-up: once it has finished they reuse the prepared state, and before then they take the ordinary path. The warm-up is bounded by the analysis budget and may not complete on every input.

On Unix, after a field run on an input of at least 16 MiB that takes longer than 250 ms, the CLI starts a background xref -b BIN field-daemon for that binary. It keeps the image and the field session in memory behind a private socket in ./field-index-v1/daemon/, and later xref field runs for the same unchanged binary and xref executable are answered by it without reloading the image (stderr says field daemon). It re-checks the input and executable metadata before every request and exits when either changed or after XREF_FIELD_DAEMON_IDLE_SECS (default 900) without requests. XREF_NO_DAEMON=1 disables it.

A repeated field command with exactly the same arguments on an unchanged input replays the stored report from .../field-index-v1/results without loading or hashing the image. The key covers every argument, the canonical input path and its device, inode, size, modification and change times, and the same metadata of the xref executable. Reports that hit the 30-second analysis budget are not stored. Set XREF_NO_RESULT_CACHE=1 to bypass it. A query with different arguments runs the search again; the selected context functions are analysed in parallel.

For a repeatable Linux x86-64 stress case, the repository can generate a neutral ELF with 65,000 additional functions. The --writers variant makes each of them write the same two offsets, stressing ranking before the limit:

Command
python3 tests/fixtures/field_perf/generate.py /tmp/xref-field-perf --writers
cc -O2 -g0 -fno-inline -fno-ipa-icf /tmp/xref-field-perf/target.c /tmp/xref-field-perf/bulk.S -o /tmp/xref-field-perf/target
objcopy --strip-all /tmp/xref-field-perf/target /tmp/xref-field-perf/target-stripped
xref -b /tmp/xref-field-perf/target-stripped field --keys c,m,e --write --writes-all-of m,e --limit 1

Run the last command twice to distinguish index construction from reuse. The generated code is synthetic and timings do not predict performance for every real binary.
